newsitem.title: UK: Seven injured in Northern Ireland attacks.
newsitem.headline: Seven injured in Northern Ireland attacks.

text.p: Seven people -- two teenagers and five members of a joint police and British army patrol -- were injured in attacks in the Northern Ireland capital Belfast overnight, police said on Saturday.
The teenagers, one aged 14 and the other 18, were hurt in shootings early on Saturday as Protestants marked the "Glorious 12th of July" with bonfires, fireworks and music.

The festivities, accompanied by parades by the staunchly Protestant Orange Order, commemorate a 1690 victory over Catholic forces at the Battle of the Boyne and are a considerable irritant to Northern Ireland's Catholic minority.
Three soldiers and two police officers were injured on Friday night when their security force patrol came under a gun and bomb attack believed to have been carried out by republican guerrillas.
"We have got five casualties, both Royal Ulster Constabulary and military. It happened in a terrorist attack,"said a police spokesman.
None of those hurt in the attacks were reported to have suffered life-threatening injuries.
Earlier, tensions in Northern Ireland appeared to have subsided after the Orange Order announced it was cancelling four flashpoint parades in Belfast and other towns.

Cecil Walker, a Belfast member of parliament for the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party, said the attack was a bitter disappointment after the Orange Order's decision to cancel its contentious parades.
"We were hoping things were going to be better than they were," he told reporters at the scene of the attack.
"But there are obviously elements in the nationalist community who seem to be holding on to mayhem."

The gesture to cancel or reroute disputed parades in Belfast, Armagh, Newry and Londonderry was widely praised in a province which had feared the marches could cause major unrest between Protestant and Irish nationalist Catholic communities.
A decision by police chiefs to allow the Orange Order to march along Portadown's Catholic Garvaghy Road last Sunday sparked several days of the worst violence seen in Northern Ireland for many years.
Nationalists in Belfast and Londonderry had threatened to stage massive counter demonstrations if Orangemen were allowed to stage marches on Saturday.

The Orange Order's decision to call off the four potentially violent parades rekindled hopes that the Irish Republican Army (IRA) would match the concession with a new ceasefire in its war to end British rule in Northern Ireland.

Gerry Adams, president of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, welcomed the unprecedented scrapping of some of the Protestant order's most cherished processions but refused to speculate on the likelihood of a new truce.
"I am not going to speculate about the IRA. I cannot speculate about how the IRA will respond to these developments," Adams told a Belfast news conference.

The decision over the parades exposed rifts within the Orange Order, with hardliners calling on pro-British Unionist political leaders to pull out of peace talks sponsored by the British and Irish governments.
Ulster Unionist leader David Trimble said he would consider what the Orangemen had to say about the peace talks.
There was still friction in the mainly Catholic villages of Dunloy and Bellaghy where anti-parade feeling has been running high for some weeks.
But in the town of Newtownbutler, Catholics and Protestants reached a compromise about a Saturday parade.
